entry.gloss: how each voice moves from chord to chord
entry.def: The way the individual voices, or parts, move from one chord to the next. Good voice leading in common-practice style keeps each voice singable: common tones are held, other voices move by step where possible, and parallel fifths and octaves are avoided. Also called part writing.

figure.caption: The soprano holds the common tone C; the alto and tenor move by step.

entry.gloss: soprano, alto, tenor and bass: four-part texture
entry.def: Soprano, alto, tenor and bass: the four voices of a mixed choir, and the four-part texture in which harmony is traditionally taught. Written on a grand staff, the soprano and alto share the treble staff with stems up and down, and the tenor and bass share the bass staff.

entry.gloss: highest of the four voices
entry.def: The highest voice of four-part writing, which usually carries the melody. Its range in harmony exercises is about C4 to G5, a little higher in some books. One of the two outer voices.

entry.gloss: second-highest of the four voices
entry.def: The second-highest voice of four-part writing, written on the treble staff with stems down. Its range in harmony exercises is about G3 to C5 or D5.

entry.gloss: second-lowest of the four voices
entry.def: The second-lowest voice of four-part writing, written on the bass staff with stems up in harmony exercises, or in choral scores on a treble staff that sounds an octave lower. Its range is about C3 to G4 or A4.

figure.caption: The tenor range written in the octave treble clef.

entry.gloss: lowest of the four voices
entry.def: The lowest voice of four-part writing, which carries the harmony's foundation and decides the chord's inversion. Its range in harmony exercises is about E2 to C4 or D4. One of the two outer voices.

entry.gloss: span from a voice's lowest to highest note
entry.def: The span of notes a voice or instrument can sing or play. Harmony exercises keep each voice within a comfortable range: roughly C4–G5 for the soprano, G3–C5 for the alto, C3–G4 for the tenor and E2–C4 for the bass; textbooks differ by a step or so at the edges. The part of the range where a voice is most comfortable is its tessitura.

entry.gloss: the soprano and the bass
entry.def: The highest and lowest voices, the soprano and the bass. Listeners hear them best, so their counterpoint matters most: contrary motion and imperfect consonances between them are preferred, and direct fifths and octaves with a leaping soprano are avoided between them.

entry.gloss: the alto and the tenor
entry.def: The voices between the soprano and the bass, in four-part writing the alto and the tenor. They fill in the harmony and should move as smoothly as possible, often by holding common tones.

entry.gloss: distances between neighboring voices
entry.def: The distances between neighboring voices of a chord. In four-part writing the soprano and alto, and the alto and tenor, are normally no more than an octave apart, while the tenor and bass may be farther apart.

figure.caption: Upper voices within an octave of each other; a wide gap between tenor and bass.

entry.gloss: upper three voices within an octave
entry.def: A spacing in which the soprano and tenor are less than an octave apart, so no chord note could be put between the upper three voices. Also called close structure or close spacing.

entry.gloss: soprano and tenor an octave or more apart
entry.def: A spacing in which the soprano and tenor are an octave or more apart, leaving room for chord notes between the upper voices. Also called open structure or open spacing.

entry.gloss: three voices in the right hand, the bass in the left
entry.def: A four-part texture written for the piano, with the three upper voices close together on the treble staff for the right hand and the bass alone on the bass staff for the left. In chorale style, by contrast, two voices share each staff.

entry.gloss: two voices sharing one chord note
entry.def: Giving one note of a triad to two voices, in unison or octaves, as four-part writing must. In root position the root is usually doubled; in second inversion the bass. The leading tone and the seventh of a chord are not doubled, since each has only one good resolution.

figure.caption: The root, C, doubled by the bass and the soprano.

entry.gloss: two voices moving the same way, same interval
entry.def: Two voices move in parallel when they move in the same direction and keep the same interval number between them, such as two voices a third or a sixth apart. Parallel thirds and sixths are common; parallel fifths and octaves are avoided.

entry.gloss: two voices moving the same way, changing interval
entry.def: Two voices move in similar motion when they move in the same direction by different intervals, so the interval between them changes.

figure.caption: Both voices rise, from a fifth to a sixth.

entry.gloss: two voices moving in opposite directions
entry.def: Two voices move in contrary motion when one rises while the other falls. It keeps the voices independent and is the preferred motion between the outer voices.

entry.gloss: one voice moves while the other stays
entry.def: Two voices move in oblique motion when one of them keeps its pitch while the other moves up or down.

entry.gloss: two voices moving from one perfect fifth to another
entry.def: Two voices a perfect fifth (or a twelfth) apart that both move to another perfect fifth. They are avoided in common-practice part writing because they weaken the independence of the voices. Called consecutive fifths in British English; fifths by contrary motion, as from a fifth to a twelfth, are usually avoided too.

entry.gloss: two voices moving from one octave to another
entry.def: Two voices an octave (or a unison) apart that both move to another octave on a different note: the two voices then sound like one. They are avoided in part writing, though doubling a whole line in octaves, as orchestras do, is a different thing. Called consecutive octaves in British English.

entry.gloss: outer voices reaching a fifth by similar motion
entry.def: A perfect fifth reached by similar motion. Between the outer voices it is avoided when the soprano leaps, and allowed when the soprano moves by step. Also called hidden fifths.

figure.caption: Both voices rise into the fifth F–C, the upper one by leap.

entry.gloss: outer voices reaching an octave by similar motion
entry.def: An octave reached by similar motion. Like direct fifths, it is avoided between the outer voices unless the soprano moves by step. Also called hidden octaves.

entry.gloss: a perfect and a diminished fifth in succession
entry.def: Two voices moving from a perfect fifth to a diminished fifth, or the reverse. A perfect fifth moving to a diminished fifth is generally allowed; a diminished fifth moving to a perfect fifth is avoided, at least when one voice is the bass, because the diminished fifth should resolve inward to a third.

figure.caption: A diminished fifth moving to a perfect fifth instead of resolving to the third C–E.

entry.gloss: a voice moving above a higher or below a lower one
entry.def: A voice goes above the voice normally higher than it, or below the voice normally lower, such as the alto above the soprano. It is avoided in four-part exercises because the listener can no longer follow the lines.

entry.gloss: a voice passing the neighboring voice's previous note
entry.def: A voice moves above the note that the next higher voice has just left, or below the note the next lower voice has just left, without actually crossing it: the tenor rising to E4 just after the alto has left D4. It is avoided for the same reason as voice crossing.

entry.gloss: note that strongly pulls in one direction
entry.def: A note with a strong pull to move to a particular next note: the leading tone up to the tonic, the seventh of a chord down by step, and chromatically raised or lowered notes in the direction of their alteration. Tendency tones are not doubled.

figure.caption: In V7–I, the leading tone B rises to C and the seventh F falls to E.

entry.gloss: a dissonance moving to a consonance
entry.def: The move from a dissonance to a consonance, usually by step, and the note reached by that move: the seventh of V7 resolves down to the third of I. A dissonance that moves elsewhere is said to be unresolved.

figure.caption: The augmented fourth F–B resolves outward to the sixth E–C.

entry.gloss: note shared by two successive chords
entry.def: A note that belongs to two successive chords, such as C in I and IV of C major. In smooth voice leading it is usually kept in the same voice.

figure.caption: C, common to both chords, stays in the soprano.

entry.gloss: leading tone falling to the fifth in an inner voice
entry.def: A leading tone in an inner voice that falls to the fifth of the tonic chord instead of rising to the tonic, so that the final chord is complete. It is allowed in an inner voice at V–I, but not in the soprano.

figure.caption: The tenor falls from B to G; rising to C would leave the tonic triad without its fifth.

entry.gloss: 6/4 chord over a bass passing by step
entry.def: A second-inversion chord on a weak beat over a bass that passes by step between two positions of one chord, as in I–V6/4–I6. The voices above it usually move by step, often in a voice exchange with the bass.

entry.gloss: 6/4 chord over a held or repeated bass
entry.def: A second-inversion chord over a bass note that is held or repeated, while two upper voices rise by step and return, as in I–IV6/4–I. Also called a neighboring six-four.

entry.gloss: 6/4 made by a bass arpeggiating one chord
entry.def: A second-inversion chord that arises when the bass moves through the notes of a chord that is held above it, as in waltz and march accompaniments.
